sections.h2: Where is Madison, Mississippi, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Madison sits in southern Madison County, about 13 miles north of Jackson, and it is part of the Jackson metropolitan area. The city borders Ridgeland to the south, and Gluckstadt lies roughly 5 miles to the north.

Interstate 55 runs through the city with exits at Madison Avenue (Exit 107) and Highway 463 (Exit 108). U.S. 51 crosses the older center of town, and the Natchez Trace Parkway follows the eastern edge. Highway 463 is the main business corridor.

The city covers about 26.4 square miles, and water makes up a little over 4 percent of that. The east side drains toward the Ross Barnett Reservoir on the Pearl River. The north drains to Bear Creek and the west to Limekiln Creek, both of which feed the Big Black River system. If your lot backs onto a creek or a drainage easement, a buyer's inspector will notice it, so be ready to explain it.

sections.h2: How did Madison grow into a city?
sections.html:
Madison began in 1856 as a railroad stop. The Illinois Central Railroad opened Madison Station that year, and the older stagecoach settlement of Madisonville, which had served as the first Madison County seat in 1828, slowly emptied as residents moved to the rail line.

The town was badly damaged during the 1863 siege of Jackson, and it recovered slowly. For most of the twentieth century it stayed small. The 1950 census counted 540 people. By 1990 the count was 7,471, and by 2000 it was 14,692. After years of court battles, the city also annexed territory in the late 2000s to expand its limits.

That growth is recent. Most of the city's population arrived after 1980, so a large share of its houses are newer than in many Mississippi towns. If your neighborhood has a homeowners association, ask it early for any resale paperwork it requires, since the city ties some permits to association approval.

sections.h2: What does a tornado, hail or heavy rain mean for a Madison house?
sections.html:
Severe weather is the main physical risk to a Madison roof. On November 24, 2001, an F4 tornado hit the western part of the city, leveled homes in the Fairfield subdivision, and damaged or destroyed 164 homes along an 11.5 mile path through Madison County. Two people died and 21 were injured.

That event is the best documented example of what a strong storm does here. If your house has an old patch, a sagging ridge line or a past insurance claim, gather the paperwork before you list or accept any offer.

Under Madison's permit rules, roofs, foundation work, fences, pools and demolition all need permits. If a previous owner skipped one, the gap can surface at inspection. A buyer who pays cash and plans to renovate usually prices that risk in rather than asking you to fix it first.

sections.h2: What city rules should a Madison seller know about?
sections.html:
Madison enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, and the city has a dedicated code compliance officer. The building department lists permit requirements for new homes, additions and renovations, foundations, roofs, fences, pools, demolition, and rental property. Gas and electric permits are issued when utilities have been off for more than six months, which matters for a house that has sat vacant.

The city's code pages cover housing condition, litter, signs, overgrowth, nuisance and vehicle complaints. The vehicle rule is specific: no inoperative or unlicensed vehicle may be parked or kept on a premises, and a vehicle in major disassembly is not allowed outside an enclosed structure.

Madison opened a municipal environmental court in January 2019 to hear code cases. At the time, the Clarion-Ledger reported that an owner who ignored a notice could face a fine of up to $1,000 per day and up to 90 days in jail. Confirm current penalties with the city, but the lesson for sellers is simple: an open violation on an inherited or vacant house gets worse with time.

  • Check the city's code violation form and ask whether any complaint is open on your address.
  • If a homeowners association exists, the city's property maintenance code states that a permit will not be issued without the association's written approval.
  • Keep copies of past permits for roofs, additions and pools.
  • Report utilities that have been off for months, since the city will want a permit to turn gas or electric back on.

You can read the rules on the City of Madison building and permits page.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work when you sell a house in Madison?
sections.html:
Property taxes on a Madison house are billed by Madison County and are due by February 1 of the following year. Mississippi assesses property each January 1 to the owner of record, and the tax bill arrives in November or December. If February 1 lands on a weekend or holiday, you can pay the next Monday without penalty.

A single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I property and is assessed at 10 percent of its value. Other real property, such as a rental house, is Class II at 15 percent. A home in Madison also pays a county rate, a school district rate and a city rate, because it lies inside city limits.

The state example shows how the math runs: a $100,000 home at 10 percent gives $10,000 in assessed value, and at 125 mills that is $1,250. Closing agents usually prorate the current year between buyer and seller. To dispute a valuation, ask the Madison County chancery clerk for a Board of Supervisors hearing, normally by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due.

The Mississippi Secretary of State's county directory lists the Madison County tax collector at 146 W. Center Street in Canton. Ask there for payoff figures on any back taxes before you close.

sections.h2: What disclosure rules apply when you sell a house in Madison?
sections.html:
Mississippi requires most sellers to hand the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement. Under Mississippi Code section 89-1-503, the seller delivers it as soon as practicable before title transfers. If it arrives after an offer is made, the buyer has three days after hand delivery, or five days after mailing, to cancel the offer in writing.

A seller who skips the form does not escape the issue. The statute says a buyer who gets no statement is presumed to be on notice to ask the seller about the property. Cash buyers who buy as-is still ask about roofs, drainage, termites, flooding and past repairs, so honest answers on paper save time on both sides.

The state's homestead exemption also affects a Madison sale. Homeowners must apply with the county tax assessor between January 1 and April 1, and a change in ownership or occupancy can trigger a new application for the buyer. Ownership must be recorded with the chancery clerk before January 7 for the exemption to apply that year, so a late-year closing is worth planning around.

sections.h2: What are your options for selling a house in Madison?
sections.html:
Madison sellers usually choose between a traditional listing, a sale without an agent, or a cash offer from an investor. A listing can bring the highest price when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings, inspections and a lender's appraisal. A cash buyer trades some of that price for speed, fewer contingencies and no repair demands.

  • Listing: best for updated homes in sought-after neighborhoods, with a longer timeline.
  • For sale by owner: saves a commission but puts the disclosure form, contract and negotiation on you.
  • Cash sale: fits inherited houses, tenant-occupied homes, code violations, deferred roofs and tight deadlines.

Madison is known for its appearance standards, which means a neglected house stands out to neighbors and to code staff. That is a reason many owners of vacant or inherited homes choose to sell quickly rather than carry the taxes, insurance and mowing. Madison County School District and nearby private schools, including Madison-Ridgeland Academy, also draw families, so a well-kept house in the right subdivision can still do well on the open market.

If you want a number without commitment, we can review the address and explain how a cash offer works. You owe nothing if you decline.

faqs.q: How far is Madison, MS from Jackson?
faqs.a: Madison is about 13 miles north of Jackson. Interstate 55 connects the two, with Madison exits at Madison Avenue and Highway 463.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due on a house in Madison, MS?
faqs.a: Property taxes are due by February 1 of the year after the January 1 assessment. If February 1 falls on a weekend or holiday, you can pay the following Monday without penalties. Bills go out in November or December.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Madison?
faqs.a: Yes. The City of Madison building and permits department lists roofs among the work that requires a permit. Fences, foundation work, pools and demolition also need one.

faqs.q: What happens if a Madison house has a code violation?
faqs.a: The city's code compliance officer notifies the owner and gives time to fix it. If the problem is not corrected, the case can go to Madison's environmental court, which started in 2019. Contact the city to confirm the current process and penalties.

faqs.q: Must I give a buyer a disclosure statement in Mississippi?
faqs.a: In most sales, yes. Section 89-1-503 requires delivery of the written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before title transfers. A buyer who receives it after making an offer has three days in person or five days by mail to withdraw.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Madison, MS as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer will typically purchase a house as-is, with no repairs requested. You still need legal authority to sell, so ask the chancery clerk or an attorney about estate paperwork first.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Madison?
faqs.a: Madison County collects it. The county tax collector's listing from the Mississippi Secretary of State is at 146 W. Center Street, Canton. The county tax assessor values the property and the chancery clerk keeps deed records.
